by_sid.pliny_6_16.0: You ask that I write to you about the death of my uncle, so that you may be able to hand it down to posterity more truthfully.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.1: I thank you; for I see that, if his death is celebrated by you, an immortal glory has been set forth for it.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.2: For although he perished in the destruction of the most beautiful of lands, like peoples, like cities perish in memorable disaster, as if destined to live forever, and although he himself founded many enduring works, nevertheless the eternity of your writings will add much to his perpetuity.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.3: I consider those blessed, indeed, to whom it has been given by the gift of the gods either to do things worth writing about or to write things worth reading, but those most blessed to whom both have been given.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.4: Among the number of these my uncle will be, both through his own books and through yours.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.5: And so I undertake the more willingly, I even demand, what you enjoin.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.6: He was at Misenum and was commanding the fleet in person with full authority.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.7: On the ninth day before the Kalends of September, around the seventh hour, my mother points out to him that a cloud is appearing, unusual in both size and shape.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.8: He, having taken the sun, then a cold bath, had eaten lying down and was studying; he asks for his sandals and climbs to a place from which that marvel could best be observed.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.9: A cloud was rising — it was unclear to those watching from afar from which mountain (it was later known to have been Vesuvius) — and no tree could more closely express its likeness and shape than the pine.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.10: For lifted up to a great height as if on a very long trunk, it spread out into branches, I suppose because it was carried up by a fresh blast, then, as that blast weakened, the cloud was left unsupported, or even overcome by its own weight, and was dispersing laterally, sometimes white, sometimes dirty and spotted, depending on whether it had carried up earth or ash.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.11: It seemed to him, as a most learned man, a great matter and one to be examined more closely.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.12: He orders a swift boat to be made ready; he gives me the opportunity to come along if I wish; I replied that I preferred to study, and by chance he himself had given me something to write.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.13: He was going out of the house; he receives a note from Rectina, the wife of Tascus, terrified by the imminent danger (for her villa lay below the mountain, and there was no escape except by ship): she begged that he rescue her from such great peril.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.14: He changed his plan, and what he had begun in a scholarly spirit he carried out in the greatest one.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.15: He launches the quadriremes and embarks himself, intending to bring help not only to Rectina but to many (for the pleasantness of the coast was popular).
by_sid.pliny_6_16.16: He hurries to the place from which others are fleeing, and holds a straight course and straight rudders into the danger, so free from fear that he was dictating and noting down every motion, every shape of that disaster as he had grasped them with his eyes.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.17: Already ash was falling on the ships, the closer they approached, the hotter and denser; already pumice stones too and stones blackened and burned and shattered by fire; already a sudden shallow and shores blocked by the collapse of the mountain.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.18: Having hesitated a little whether to turn back, then, when the helmsman was advising him to do so, he said, 'Fortune favors the brave: make for Pomponianus.'
by_sid.pliny_6_16.19: He was at Stabiae, separated by the middle of the bay (for the sea pours in along shores that gradually curve and bend); there, although the danger was not yet near, but in plain sight and, as it grew, very close, he had loaded his belongings onto ships, resolved on flight if the contrary wind should die down.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.20: Carried in by this most favorable wind, my uncle then embraces him as he trembles, consoles him, encourages him, and so that he might soothe his fear by his own calm, orders himself to be carried into the bath; bathed, he reclines and dines, either cheerful or (which is equally great) seeming cheerful.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.21: Meanwhile, from Mount Vesuvius in several places very wide flames and tall fires were shining out, whose brightness and clarity was made greater by the darkness of the night.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.22: He, to remedy their fear, kept saying that the fires were left behind by the panic of the country folk and that the abandoned villas were burning in the desolation.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.23: Then he gave himself to rest and rested in a most genuine sleep; for the passage of his breath, which was heavier and more sonorous in him because of his bulk, was heard by those who were near the threshold.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.24: But the courtyard from which the room was entered had now risen so high, filled with ash mixed with pumice, that if the delay in the bedroom were longer, exit would be denied.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.25: Awakened, he comes out and rejoins Pomponianus and the others who had stayed up all night.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.26: They consult together, whether to remain inside the buildings or wander in the open.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.27: For the buildings were swaying with frequent and vast tremors, and seemed, as if torn from their foundations, to be moving now here, now there, or being carried back.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.28: Under the open sky, on the other hand, the fall of light and porous pumice stones was feared, but a comparison of the dangers settled on this; with him indeed reason overcame reason, with the others fear overcame fear.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.29: They tie pillows on their heads with cloths; this was a defense against the falling debris.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.30: Day was now elsewhere, there a night blacker and denser than any night; this, however, many torches and various lights relieved.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.31: It was decided to go out to the shore and to see from close up whether the sea would yet allow anything; it still remained vast and contrary.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.32: There, lying down on a thrown-down cloth, he asked for cold water once and again and drank it.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.33: Then flames, and the smell of sulfur announcing flames, turn the others to flight and rouse him.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.34: Leaning on two slaves, he stood up and immediately collapsed, as I gather, his breathing being obstructed by the thicker fumes and his throat being closed, which by nature was weak and narrow and frequently inflamed.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.35: When daylight returned (the third from the day he had last seen), his body was found whole, unharmed, and clothed as he had been when dressed: the appearance of the body more like one resting than one dead.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.36: Meanwhile at Misenum I and my mother — but nothing to do with history, nor did you wish to know anything other than about his death.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.37: Therefore I will make an end.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.38: I will add one thing, that I have followed up on everything I was present for and everything I had heard immediately afterwards, when the truest things are remembered.
by_sid.pliny_6_16.39: You will pick out the most important parts; for it is one thing to write a letter, another to write history, one thing to write to a friend, another to write to everyone.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.0: Leisure provides both me with the chance to learn and you with the chance to teach.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.1: Therefore I would very much like to know whether you think that ghosts exist and have their own form and some divine power, or whether they are empty and unreal and take their image from our fear.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.2: I am led to believe that they exist chiefly by what I hear happened to Curtius Rufus.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.3: Still poor and unknown, he had attached himself as a companion to the man holding Africa as governor.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.4: As the day was waning he was walking in a portico; the figure of a woman, larger and more beautiful than human, presented herself to him.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.5: To him in his terror she said she was Africa, foreteller of things to come: for he would go to Rome, and would hold offices, and would even return to the same province with the highest command, and there he would die.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.6: All these things came to pass.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.7: Furthermore, as he was approaching Carthage and getting off the ship, the same figure is said to have met him on the shore.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.8: He himself, certainly, when he was caught up in illness, judging the future from the past, the bad from the good, threw away all hope of recovery, though none of his own people was despairing.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.9: Now is not this story I will tell as I received it both more terrifying and no less wonderful?
by_sid.pliny_7_27.10: There was at Athens a spacious and roomy house, but ill-omened and unhealthy.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.11: Through the silence of the night the sound of iron, and if you listened more carefully, the rattling of chains was given back, at first further off, then close at hand: soon a phantom appeared, an old man wasted with thinness and squalor, with a long beard and bristling hair; on his legs he wore fetters, on his hands chains, and he kept rattling them.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.12: Hence sad and dreadful nights were passed sleepless by the inhabitants through fear; illness followed the sleeplessness, and as the dread grew, death.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.13: For even by day, although the apparition had withdrawn, the memory of the apparition wandered before their eyes, and the fear was longer-lasting than its causes.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.14: Hence the house was deserted and condemned to solitude and left entirely to that monster; nevertheless it was advertised, in case anyone unaware of such a great evil should wish to buy or to rent it.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.15: The philosopher Athenodorus came to Athens, read the placard, and when he heard the price, since the cheapness was suspicious, he inquired and was told everything, and rents it nonetheless, indeed all the more.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.16: When it began to grow dark, he orders a couch to be made for him in the front part of the house; he asks for tablets, a stylus, a lamp; he sends all his people into the inner rooms; he himself directs his mind, eyes, and hand to writing, lest his empty mind should fashion for itself the apparitions he had heard about and empty fears.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.17: At first, the silence of the night, such as everywhere; then iron rattles, chains are moved.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.18: He does not lift his eyes, does not put down his stylus, but steels his mind and stops up his ears.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.19: Then the noise grew louder, came nearer, and was now heard as if at the threshold, now as if within the threshold.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.20: He looks back, sees, and recognizes the figure that had been described to him.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.21: It was standing and was beckoning with its finger like one calling.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.22: He, on the contrary, signals with his hand that it should wait a moment, and again leans over his wax tablets and stylus; the figure was rattling its chains over the head of the writer.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.23: He looks back again, the apparition beckoning the same way as before, and without delay he picks up the lamp and follows.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.24: It went with a slow step as if heavy with its chains.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.25: After it turned aside into the courtyard of the house, suddenly it slipped away and abandoned its companion.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.26: Left alone, he places plucked grass and leaves as a marker on the spot.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.27: On the next day he goes to the magistrates and advises them to order that place to be dug up.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.28: Bones are found, set into chains and entwined, which the body, decayed by age and earth, had left bare and gnawed away in their fetters; gathered up, they are buried at public expense.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.29: After the spirits were duly laid to rest, the house was free.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.30: These things indeed I believe on the testimony of those who affirm them; the following I can affirm to others.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.31: I have a freedman who is not unlettered.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.32: His younger brother used to sleep in the same bed with him.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.33: He seemed to himself to see someone sitting on the bed and bringing scissors to his head, and even cutting off hair from the very crown.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.34: When day broke, he himself was found shorn around the crown, and the cut hair was found lying there.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.35: A short interval of time, and again something similar gave credibility to the first event.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.36: A boy was sleeping in the slave-quarters mixed in with many others.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.37: Two figures came in through the windows (so he relates) in white tunics, and they sheared the boy as he lay and went back the way they had come.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.38: Day showed this boy too shorn and the hair scattered around him.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.39: Nothing notable followed, except perhaps that I was not put on trial, though I would have been, if Domitian, under whom these things happened, had lived longer.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.40: For in his writing-case was found a charge brought against me by Carus; from which it can be conjectured that, since it is the custom for defendants to let their hair grow, the cutting of my people's hair was a sign of the danger which was threatening having been averted.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.41: Therefore I ask you to apply your learning.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.42: The matter is worthy of long and serious consideration; nor am I myself unworthy that you should share with me the abundance of your knowledge.
by_sid.pliny_7_27.43: You may even argue both sides of the case (as you usually do), but argue the more strongly on one side, lest you send me away in suspense and uncertainty, since the reason for consulting you was that I might cease to doubt.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.0: It is my custom, lord, to refer to you all matters about which I am in doubt.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.1: For who can better either guide my hesitation or instruct my ignorance?
by_sid.pliny_10_96.2: I have never been present at trials of Christians: therefore I do not know what is usually punished or investigated, or to what extent.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.3: Nor have I hesitated only a little: whether there is any distinction of ages, or whether however young they are they differ in no way from the stronger; whether pardon is to be granted to repentance, or whether for one who has been a Christian at all it does no good to have ceased; whether the name itself, even if it lacks crimes, or only the crimes attached to the name, should be punished.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.4: Meanwhile, with those who were brought before me as Christians, I have followed this method.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.5: I asked them whether they were Christians.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.6: Those who confessed I asked a second and a third time, threatening punishment: those who persisted I ordered to be led away to execution.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.7: For I did not doubt that, whatever it was that they were confessing, their stubbornness certainly and inflexible obstinacy ought to be punished.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.8: There were others of similar madness, whom, because they were Roman citizens, I noted as needing to be sent back to the City.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.9: Soon, in the very course of the proceedings, as is usually the case, the charge spreading itself, more variations arose.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.10: An anonymous document was put forward containing the names of many people.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.11: Those who denied that they were or had been Christians, when, with me leading them, they invoked the gods and made supplication with incense and wine to your image, which I had ordered to be brought in for this purpose along with the statues of the gods, and besides cursed Christ — none of which, it is said, those who are truly Christians can be compelled to do — I thought should be released.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.12: Others named by an informer said that they were Christians and then denied it; they had been, indeed, but had ceased, some three years before, some many years before, a few even twenty years before.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.13: These too all venerated both your image and the statues of the gods and cursed Christ.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.14: They asserted, however, that this had been the sum of their fault or error: that they had been accustomed to meet on a fixed day before dawn and to recite a hymn antiphonally to Christ as to a god, and to bind themselves by oath not to any crime, but that they would not commit thefts, robberies, or adulteries, that they would not break their word, that they would not deny a deposit when called upon to return it.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.15: When these things had been done, it had been their custom to depart and gather again to take food, but ordinary and harmless food; and even this they had ceased to do after my edict, by which, according to your instructions, I had forbidden secret societies.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.16: On account of this I believed it all the more necessary to seek the truth from two slave-women, who were called deaconesses, even by means of torture.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.17: I found nothing other than a depraved and excessive superstition.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.18: Therefore, postponing the inquiry, I have hastened to consult you.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.19: For the matter has seemed to me worthy of consultation, especially because of the number of those at risk.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.20: For many of every age, of every rank, of both sexes also are being called and will be called into danger.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.21: And not only cities, but villages too and country districts have been pervaded by the contagion of this superstition; which seems able to be checked and corrected.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.22: Certainly it is sufficiently agreed that the temples, almost already deserted, have begun to be frequented again, and that the customary rites long interrupted are being resumed, and that everywhere sacrificial victims are being sold, of which until recently a buyer was very rarely found.
by_sid.pliny_10_96.23: From which it is easy to suppose what a crowd of people could be set right, if there were a place for repentance.
by_sid.pliny_10_97.0: You have followed the procedure, my Secundus, that you ought to have followed in examining the cases of those who had been brought before you as Christians.
by_sid.pliny_10_97.1: For nothing can be laid down as a general rule which has, so to speak, a fixed form.
by_sid.pliny_10_97.2: They are not to be hunted out; if they are brought before you and convicted, they are to be punished, but in such a way that one who denies that he is a Christian and makes this clear by the very deed itself, that is, by supplicating our gods, although suspect with regard to the past, may obtain pardon through repentance.
by_sid.pliny_10_97.3: But anonymous documents put forward should have no place in any charge.
by_sid.pliny_10_97.4: For it is both of the worst precedent and not in keeping with our age.
by_sid.pliny_6_4.0: Never have I complained more about my own duties, which did not allow me either to accompany you as you set out for Campania for your health, or to follow you immediately after you had set out.
by_sid.pliny_6_4.1: For now especially I was longing to be with you, so that I might trust my own eyes about what you were managing for your strength, what for your dear body, and finally whether you were getting through the pleasures of your retreat and the abundance of the region without trouble.
by_sid.pliny_6_4.2: Indeed I should miss you, even when strong, not without anxiety; for it is suspenseful and worrying to know nothing for a time about one whom you love most ardently.
by_sid.pliny_6_4.3: But now the thought both of your absence and of your illness alarms me with uncertain and varied worry.
by_sid.pliny_6_4.4: I fear everything, I imagine everything, and as is the nature of those who are afraid, I picture to myself most vividly the very things I most dread.
by_sid.pliny_6_4.5: Therefore I beg you all the more earnestly to attend to my fear daily by one or even two letters.
by_sid.pliny_6_4.6: For I shall be more at ease while I read, and shall fear again as soon as I have finished reading.
